passage: Asif, you keep asking if I'm okay. I keep saying fine. And I mean it, sort of. Nothing happened. I'm Irawati, I'm always fine, right? It's just, my head's been aching every afternoon for two weeks. My shoulders feel like someone's standing on them. I can't sleep till two, and in the morning my stomach's too knotted for breakfast. Mummy asked if I'm sad about Nani moving to Pune. I said no. I don't think so? When I try to work out what I'm feeling, it's like opening a cupboard and it's just dark in there. So I say fine. Is that weird? Maybe my body knows something I don't. Okay. If you sit with me, I'll tell Mummy tonight about the headaches. And maybe the cupboard. That evening Irawati told Mummy everything, Asif sitting close. Mummy listened, then said, "None of this is your fault. We'll see the doctor this week."

qa.q: How long has Irawati's head been aching every afternoon?
qa.a: For two weeks.

qa.q: What does the dark cupboard image suggest about Irawati's feelings?
qa.a: It suggests Irawati has real feelings, perhaps sadness about Nani moving, but no words to reach them, so only the body shows it.

qa.q: Why was telling Mummy that same evening a good step for Irawati?
qa.a: It let an adult hear about the headaches and sleeplessness right away; Mummy listened, said it was not Irawati's fault and planned a doctor visit.

qa.q: How might Asif feel hearing all this after only ever getting "fine"?
qa.a: Asif may feel relieved to finally understand and worried about the aches, and glad to be trusted with it.

grounding: A teenager insists on being fine while describing headaches and a knotted stomach, unable to find words for feelings, and tells Mummy the same evening.

passage: I'm Lavanya, Charu's elder sister. Something's been off with her since the school exchange trip was cancelled. Every time Amma asks how she is, she says, 'Fine.' If I ask, 'Nothing.' She says it flat, not rude. But she keeps complaining about her neck, and she's stopped eating her favourite curd rice because her 'stomach feels funny.' Last night I heard her pacing at midnight. When I asked if she was upset about the trip, she looked genuinely confused. 'I don't know. I don't think so. My back hurts.' I can't tell what's going on inside her. She doesn't seem cold, more like she doesn't have the words. I told Amma tonight, and Amma is taking Charu to the doctor about the aches, and then we'll all talk.

qa.q: What has Charu stopped eating?
qa.a: Her favourite curd rice.

qa.q: What might Charu's confused look suggest when asked about the trip?
qa.a: It suggests Charu truly doesn't know what she feels; the disappointment may be showing up as neck and back aches instead of words.

qa.q: What did Lavanya choose to do, and why was it a good choice?
qa.a: Lavanya told Amma the same night, so an adult could arrange a doctor's visit for the aches and a calm family talk.

qa.q: How does Lavanya read Charu's "Fine"?
qa.a: Lavanya sees it as not cold but wordless, as if Charu lacks the words for what she feels.

grounding: An older sister notices a teenager who says fine and nothing but complains of aches, and tells their mother.

passage:
Monday. Vandana's best friend moved to Delhi. At dinner her mother, Madhuri, asked, 'How are you feeling, beta?' 'Fine.' Vandana went to bed at eight with a headache.
Thursday. 'Fine,' again, when her mother found her awake at one in the morning. 'My chest feels heavy. And my legs are tired.' Nothing about the friend.
The next Saturday. Madhuri sat on her bed with a sheet of paper listing feeling words. 'Just point, if any fit.' Vandana stared for a long time. Then, slowly, her finger went to lonely. Then to lost. She started to cry, and it felt, strangely, like relief.

qa.q: What did Madhuri bring on Saturday?
qa.a: A sheet of paper listing feeling words.

qa.q: Why did crying feel like relief to Vandana?
qa.a: Finally finding the words lonely and lost let Vandana understand the heaviness in her chest that had been there all week.

qa.q: Why was Madhuri's "Just point, if any fit" a good approach?
qa.a: It removed the pressure of explaining, letting Vandana recognise a feeling from a list instead of having to produce the words.

qa.q: What might the week have been like for Madhuri?
qa.a: Madhuri likely worried, hearing "fine" while seeing headaches and sleeplessness, and searched for a gentle way in.

grounding: Over a week, a teenager answers fine while describing aches, until her mother offers a list and she finds the words lonely and lost.

passage:
"Sabina, beti, you keep saying 'fine' to your mother. Let your Bhupen Mama tell you something.
When I was fifteen in Tezpur, my own mother asked me every evening, 'How was school?' 'Fine.' 'Why are you so quiet?' 'Nothing.' That was my whole vocabulary. And I wasn't lying. I truly didn't know what else to say.
But my body knew. My neck hurt, my stomach hurt before exams, I got headaches every Sunday night. I told the school nurse about the aches, never about anything else, because there was no anything else I could find.
Years later I realised I had been frightened of failing, and lonely after my best friend changed schools. I didn't have the words. I had a stiff neck instead.
So when you say 'fine' and then complain about your back, I don't think you're cold, Sabina. I think you're like me at fifteen."

qa.q: Where did Bhupen Mama live when he was fifteen?
qa.a: In Tezpur.

qa.q: What does Bhupen Mama think he was really feeling at fifteen?
qa.a: He thinks he was frightened of failing and lonely after his best friend changed schools, but he had no words for it and felt it as aches instead.

qa.q: What could Sabina try after hearing this story?
qa.a: She could notice when her back hurts and ask herself, or her Mama, what might be underneath, trying one word beyond 'fine' at a time.

qa.q: How might the mother in Bhupen Mama's story have felt hearing only 'fine' and 'nothing' every evening?
qa.a: She was probably worried and a little shut out, asking every evening and getting only 'fine' from a son who had grown so quiet.

grounding: It shows an elder remembering how as a teenager he answered every question with 'fine' or 'nothing' and felt aches instead of feelings, because he lacked the words.

passage:
The wedding hall in Nashik was so loud that Pradeep's ears rang. His board results had come out two days earlier, lower than anyone expected, and every relative seemed to have heard.
"Pradeep! How are you, beta?"
"Fine."
"And results?"
"Fine."
By the tenth aunty his jaw ached from smiling and his stomach felt knotted. He slipped out to the terrace, away from the band.
His cousin Chaitanya was already there, eating a samosa. "You've said 'fine' about fifty times."
"Because I am fine."
"Fine like good, or fine like nothing to say?"
Pradeep leaned on the railing. "My stomach hurts. And my head. I don't know."
"That's not nothing."
Pradeep shrugged, but he stayed. When the band started again downstairs, Chaitanya didn't go back either.

qa.q: Where did Pradeep slip out to?
qa.a: He slipped out to the terrace, away from the band.

qa.q: Why does Pradeep keep saying 'fine' though his stomach is knotted?
qa.a: He doesn't have clear words for how upset the results have left him, so 'fine' is the only answer he can find while his knotted stomach carries the rest.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya's question help at a turning point in the evening?
qa.a: Asking 'fine like good, or fine like nothing to say?' let Pradeep describe his stomach and head instead of repeating 'fine', a first step toward words.

qa.q: How might the relatives see Pradeep's repeated 'fine'?
qa.a: They may take it as polite or a bit cold and move on, not noticing the aching jaw and knotted stomach behind it.

grounding: It shows a teenager who answers every question with 'fine' and describes aches rather than feelings, not from coldness but from lacking the words.
